strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: organizing UV charts into meaningful parts and placing seams in less exposed regions could improve texture-editing workflows.

The differentiable seam-exposure objective is a plausible extension to neural parameterization. Table 1 reports lower mean seam exposure than FlexPara (0.6065 versus 0.8604), supported by qualitative seam visualizations.
Includes comparisons with neural, classical, and production tools, alongside partitioner and objective ablations. The appendix provides useful architectural details and additional examples.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to the claims. The backbone follows FlexPara, while the semantic component combines established ShDF segmentation, independent per-part parameterization, and grid packing. There is no learned semantic objective, and the discrete segmentation and packing stages do not support describing the entire framework as end-to-end differentiable.

Cross-shape semantic alignment and texture-transfer claims are unsupported. Independently fitted partitions, independently learned charts, and row-major packing do not establish consistent semantic labels, chart orientations, or UV coordinates across objects. No cross-shape correspondence or texture-transfer experiment demonstrates these properties.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified: dataset sources, mesh counts, selection criteria, aggregation procedures, and variability are absent. SAMesh predictions are treated as semantic ground truth without independent validation. Comparisons against unsegmented UV tools also conflate segmentation quality with parameterization quality; applying the same ShDF partitions before classical unwrapping is an essential missing baseline.

The geometric tradeoffs are understated. Visibility optimization reduces equiareality from 0.6759 to 0.6093 relative to the backbone; the semantic method scores 0.6707 versus xatlas's 0.9341, with lower conformality as well. These results do not substantiate claims of negligible geometric degradation. Atlas occupancy, seam length, triangle flips, and overlap rates are not reported.

Several technical claims need correction or clarification. Equation 4 defines AO as exposure, but the text surrounding Equation 7 reverses this convention and incorrectly describes the direction of the loss. Equal scaling after independently normalizing charts does not ensure consistent surface texel density. The conversion from pointwise UV predictions into valid mesh cuts, including seam-vertex duplication, is also insufficiently explained.

Perceptual benefits are evaluated mainly using the optimized AO proxy and selected checkerboard views. These do not establish improved texture generation or reduced artifacts under a defined viewpoint distribution. Comparisons with the cited visibility-aware seam-placement methods and quantitative rendered-image or user evaluations are missing.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims remain weak despite the architecture appendix. Training iterations, optimizer settings, hardware, several seam-loss hyperparameters, partition-count selection, and baseline configurations are unspecified. Reported 'inference' times do not clarify whether per-mesh optimization, segmentation, and AO preprocessing are included.

strengths: The paper addresses practical UV-mapping concerns: organizing charts around meaningful parts and placing seams in less exposed regions. Both are relevant to texture editing and content creation.

The differentiable seam-membership surrogate provides a plausible way to incorporate ambient exposure into an existing neural parameterization backbone. Table 1 reports improved mean seam exposure: 0.6065 versus 0.8604 for FlexPara and 0.7855 for OptCuts.

The paper includes multiple qualitative examples, comparisons with neural and conventional tools, partitioner ablations, and results for separate and combined objectives. The appendix provides network architectures and additional implementation details.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and insufficiently isolated. The backbone explicitly follows prior work, while the semantic pipeline combines established ShDF segmentation, independent per-part parameterization, and grid packing. There is no comparison against applying a conventional parameterizer to the same segmentation, nor experimental comparison with the cited methods specifically targeting semantic alignment or seam visibility.

The claimed end-to-end semantic objective and cross-shape correspondence are not established. Segmentation uses discrete GMM labeling, graph cuts, and post-processing; Eq. 1 contains only geometric losses. Independently learned charts and row-major packing provide no mechanism to establish consistent part identities, chart orientations, or UV coordinates across shapes. No cross-shape correspondence or texture-transfer experiment validates these claims.

The evaluation protocol is substantially underspecified. The paper does not identify the complete benchmark, its size, mesh-selection procedure, aggregation protocol, or variability across runs. Hardware, optimization schedules, and whether reported times include per-mesh training, segmentation, AO computation, and packing are unclear. Calling the timings 'inference time' is particularly ambiguous for independently optimized per-part networks.

The semantic metrics primarily measure segmentation agreement, rather than parameterization quality or cross-shape alignment. SAMesh predictions are treated as ground truth without independent validation, and comparisons against automatic chart generators confound semantic agreement with chart count and fragmentation. A controlled comparison using identical partitions is needed to establish the benefit of the proposed UV-learning stage.

Perceptual conclusions exceed the evidence. Mean seam AO closely matches the optimized objective, while checkerboard examples provide only qualitative support. There is no quantitative rendered-seam assessment under a specified camera distribution, user study, or downstream texture-generation/editing evaluation. Seam length, chart count, overlap rates, and packing efficiency are also unreported, leaving important practical tradeoffs unresolved.

The claim that geometric quality is essentially preserved understates the reported tradeoffs. Adding visibility reduces equiareality from 0.6759 to 0.6093 relative to the base model. In Table 2, the semantic variant has lower conformality and equiareality than every listed baseline; its equiareality is 0.6707 versus 0.9341 for xatlas. These results require a balanced tradeoff analysis rather than claims of improvement without harming geometry.

Several technical statements need correction or clarification. The prose surrounding Eq. 7 reverses the AO convention in Eq. 4 and describes the loss direction incorrectly, although Eq. 4 and the reported evaluation convention are mutually consistent. Equal scaling after independently normalizing each island does not ensure consistent texel density across differently sized surface parts. Moreover, pointwise vertex mappings and repulsion losses do not establish a valid, nonoverlapping triangle atlas; the procedure for cutting connectivity and duplicating seam vertices is not adequately specified or validated.

The experimental protocol is substantially underspecified. The manuscript does not identify the quantitative benchmark's size and composition, provide precise geometric metric definitions and aggregation procedures, or report variability. Optimization iterations, hardware, and whether reported times include per-object fitting and preprocessing are unclear, making the 2–15 second runtime claims difficult to assess.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the proposed parameterization method. A crucial baseline is the same ShDF partitioning followed by an established parameterizer and the same packing procedure. Without this control, semantic improvements may largely reflect the supplied segmentation. SAMesh outputs are also treated as ground truth without independent semantic validation, and directly relevant semantic- and visibility-aware prior methods discussed in related work are not experimentally compared.

The visibility formulation contains a consequential inconsistency: Equation 4 defines AO=1 as exposed, whereas the text surrounding Equation 7 reverses this convention and gives an explanation inconsistent with minimizing the displayed weighted average. Moreover, average seam AO measures the optimized proxy rather than actual perceptual visibility; no systematic viewpoint-based artifact metric or user evaluation establishes the claimed downstream benefit. Seam length and sampling-density effects are not controlled.

The claim that geometric quality is essentially preserved overstates the evidence. Adding visibility reduces equiareality from 0.6759 to 0.6093 in Table 5. In Table 2, the semantic method scores 0.6707 versus 0.9341 for xatlas, with worse conformality as well. These tradeoffs need explicit analysis rather than being characterized as negligible, particularly without quantitative texture-generation, editing, or transfer experiments.

Important atlas-validity and packing issues remain unresolved. Assigning equally scaled cells to independently normalized parts does not ensure consistent texel density across differently sized surface regions, contrary to Section 3.3. The paper also does not adequately explain seam vertex duplication or face-corner UV construction from its single-UV-per-vertex formulation, and reports no overlap, flipped-triangle, surface-coverage, or atlas-utilization measurements. Cycle consistency and vertex repulsion alone do not establish a valid bijective mesh atlas.

Central semantic claims exceed the method. Visibility evaluation largely measures the AO proxy directly optimized during training. Average seam AO does not establish reduced total visible seam length or artifacts under realistic camera and lighting distributions. Seam-length controls, held-out view-based measurements, and actual texture-generation or editing experiments are missing.

Important technical claims are unsupported. Equal scaling after independently normalizing each chart does not ensure consistent texel density across differently sized surface parts. Cycle consistency and vertex repulsion do not guarantee triangle-level injectivity, yet overlap, flipped-triangle, and surface-coverage statistics are not reported. Practical trade-offs are understated. Visibility optimization reduces equiareality from 0.6759 to 0.6093, contradicting statements that geometry is essentially unaffected. Comparing only the two-second post-training inference against OptCuts' optimization runtime in Table 1 is misleading for new-mesh processing.

strengths: The paper addresses practically relevant UV-mapping goals: meaningful chart organization and less conspicuous seams. The illustrated results demonstrate promising improvements on selected meshes.

The differentiable AO-weighted seam objective is straightforward and produces measurable improvements: Table 1 reports mean seam exposure of 0.6065, compared with 0.8604 for FlexPara and 0.7855 for OptCuts.

The evaluation includes classical and neural baselines, segmentation and packing ablations, and a 115-participant preference study. The appendix provides architecture details and per-mesh training times.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to the claims. The backbone is explicitly inherited from prior work, and the semantic pipeline combines established shape-diameter segmentation, independent per-part parameterization, and grid packing. There is no learned semantic objective or differentiation through graph-cut segmentation. Describing the complete framework as end-to-end differentiable and jointly optimizing semantic objectives is therefore misleading.

Cross-shape semantic alignment is neither established by the method nor evaluated. Independently computed segment labels, independently trained charts, and row-major packing do not ensure consistent semantic identities, chart orientations, or UV locations across objects. No correspondence or texture-transfer experiment supports this central motivation.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the proposed semantic pipeline. Essential controls include applying the same segmentation and packing to conventional parameterizers, or supplying identical partitions to FlexPara. Evaluating agreement with SAMesh outputs primarily measures partition similarity, treats predicted labels as ground truth, and does not establish improved UV mapping or downstream utility. Relevant semantic- and visibility-aware prior methods discussed in related work are also absent from the experimental comparisons.

The geometric trade-offs are substantial and sometimes understated. In Table 3, semantic-aware equiareality is 0.6707 versus 0.7606 for multi-chart FlexPara and 0.9341 for xatlas. Visibility-aware equiareality drops from 0.6759 to 0.6093 relative to single-chart FlexPara, contradicting claims that visibility optimization does not harm geometric quality. Distortion-versus-visibility trade-off curves, overlap and flipped-triangle rates, and comparable atlas-utilization measurements are needed.

Important technical claims lack adequate justification. Scaling independently normalized charts equally does not ensure consistent texel density across parts of different surface areas. Furthermore, the per-vertex mapping and soft seam detector do not explain how seam vertices are duplicated and mesh connectivity is modified to produce a valid cut mesh. Cycle consistency and vertex repulsion alone do not guarantee triangle-level bijectivity.

The experimental protocol is insufficiently specified: the aggregate benchmark's mesh count, provenance, complexity distribution, metric aggregation, hardware, and several optimization settings are unclear. The preference study reports strong results but lacks uncertainty estimates and sufficient information about presentation randomization. Its selected seam and semantic-color comparisons do not establish reduced editing effort, improved texture generation, or robust appearance across viewpoints.

The main runtime comparison obscures the cost of per-mesh optimization. Table 1 lists approximately 2 seconds for the proposed visibility method versus 240 seconds for OptCuts, but Table 9 reports average visibility-model training of 31,160 seconds, versus 1,285 seconds for FlexPara. Because training is required for each mesh, forward-pass timing alone is not a meaningful comparison of the time needed to obtain a parameterization.
